security_audit.summary: The static findings are false positives from Markdown examples and TypeScript or JSON snippets. The style template literal, callback signatures, route parameter usage, EAS command examples, and resource references are not shell execution or reconnaissance. The credential-path example does not expose a secret, but the author should clarify secret handling for copied EAS configuration.

remediation.issue: Credential path example may be copied without secret handling context.
remediation.suggestion: Clarify that service account JSON files must stay out of source control and should use EAS credentials, environment secrets, or ignored local files.

static_findings.snippet: - **Don't ignore platform differences** - Test on both iOS and Android
- If detailed examples are required, open `resources/implementation-playbook.md`.

finding_verdicts.reason: Line 484 is a TypeScript template literal used to choose a React Native style key. The variant value is constrained by the ButtonProps union, and no shell command is executed.

Line 629 shows a placeholder serviceAccountKeyPath in an eas.json example, not credential contents. The same file later tells users not to store secrets in code, although clearer secret handling guidance would help.
Line 139 reads an Expo Router route parameter in a mobile screen example. It is application state handling, not host or system reconnaissance.
Lines 443-444 define a TypeScript callback prop for a UI button. There is no system query, file access, or external process invocation.
Lines 552-553 define a ProductList callback prop for item selection. This is normal UI typing and does not inspect the execution environment.
Lines 561-562 define another typed callback in a React component example. It does not collect host information or perform reconnaissance.
Line 638 is an EAS build command shown for Android release workflows. It builds a mobile app and does not enumerate system information.
Lines 643-645 document EAS submit and update commands for app release operations. They are expected mobile deployment examples, not reconnaissance.
Lines 661-662 are best-practice prose about testing platform differences and avoiding secrets in code. The text contains no executable or investigative behavior.
Line 29 uses Markdown backticks around a documentation file path. It is an instruction to read a resource file, not Ruby or shell execution.
Line 33 uses Markdown backticks around the same resource file path. There is no command substitution or external process execution.

content.value_statement: Mobile teams need consistent Expo and React Native architecture before product code grows. This skill guides navigation, state, native APIs, offline sync, performance, and EAS release patterns.
actual_capabilities: Plan Expo project structure with app, component, hook, service, store, utility, and type layers.
Design Expo Router navigation with tabs, protected routes, dynamic routes, and programmatic navigation.
Apply authentication patterns using SecureStore and guarded route groups.
Build offline-first data flows with React Query, AsyncStorage persistence, and network status handling.
Integrate Expo native APIs for haptics, biometrics, notifications, and platform-specific UI.
Prepare EAS build, submit, and update workflows for iOS and Android releases.
limitations: Does not generate a complete app without project-specific product requirements.
Examples require adaptation for each Expo SDK, package version, and native permission model.
Does not replace testing on physical iOS and Android devices.
Release guidance does not manage real app store credentials or signing assets.

use_cases.title: Start a New Expo App
use_cases.description: Define folders, navigation groups, providers, dependencies, and setup steps before feature work begins.
use_cases.target_user: Mobile app founders and solo developers

use_cases.title: Standardize Team Architecture
use_cases.description: Align route structure, state patterns, native service boundaries, and reusable UI components across a React Native team.

use_cases.title: Prepare Mobile Releases
use_cases.description: Plan EAS build profiles, submit flows, update channels, and platform checks for iOS and Android delivery.

prompt_templates.title: Plan a New Expo App
prompt_templates.prompt: Use react-native-architecture. Plan a new Expo app for [product] with folders, navigation, authentication, core packages, and validation steps.

prompt_templates.title: Add Protected Navigation
prompt_templates.prompt: Use react-native-architecture. Design protected Expo Router navigation for [app] with auth groups, tabs, dynamic routes, and sign-in redirects.

prompt_templates.title: Design Offline Data Sync
prompt_templates.prompt: Use react-native-architecture. Propose an offline-first data flow for [feature] using React Query, AsyncStorage persistence, optimistic updates, and network status handling.

prompt_templates.title: Prepare a Production Release
prompt_templates.prompt: Use react-native-architecture. Review my React Native release plan for [app] and produce EAS build profiles, platform checks, performance risks, and rollout steps.

output_examples.input: I am starting an Expo app with authentication and tabs.
output_examples.output: A structured architecture plan covering folders, route groups, auth provider placement, tab navigation, storage choices, and setup verification.

output_examples.input: Our product list must work when users lose connection.
output_examples.output: An offline-first design with persisted queries, network awareness, optimistic mutation behavior, cache invalidation rules, and testing scenarios.

output_examples.input: We need to ship iOS and Android builds next month.
output_examples.output: A release checklist with EAS profiles, submission preparation, device testing, update channels, credential handling notes, and platform-specific risks.

best_practices: Start with Expo and EAS unless project requirements demand bare native control.
Separate navigation, providers, services, stores, reusable UI, and feature components early.
Test performance, offline behavior, permissions, and platform differences on real devices.
anti_patterns: Do not place API calls, storage writes, or expensive work directly in render paths.
Do not ignore iOS and Android differences in permissions, UI behavior, builds, and submissions.
Do not store secrets, signing assets, or service account keys in source code.

faq.question: Does this skill require Expo?
faq.answer: It focuses on Expo-first architecture, but many patterns also apply to bare React Native projects.

faq.question: Can it help with navigation design?
faq.answer: Yes. It covers Expo Router tabs, route groups, dynamic routes, protected flows, and programmatic navigation.

faq.question: Does it include offline support?
faq.answer: Yes. It includes React Query persistence, AsyncStorage caching, online status handling, and optimistic update patterns.

faq.question: Can it integrate native device features?
faq.answer: Yes. It includes examples for haptics, biometrics, notifications, permissions, and platform-specific code paths.

faq.question: Does it manage app store credentials?
faq.answer: No. It can outline release workflows, but credentials and signing assets must be handled securely by the project team.

faq.question: Is it suitable for performance reviews?
faq.answer: Yes. It can guide FlashList usage, memoization, render control, device testing, and platform performance checks.
